body.statement: Fix \(N=4\).  On a semialgebraic cell \(J\) where the channel support, confidence-primal basis, confidence-dual basis, signs of the dual positive parts, and signs of all nonzero basis denominators are fixed, any explicitly supplied certificate \(\Gamma_J\) that (i) gives primal and dual feasible solutions with a common value for a balanced binary candidate and (ii) gives, for every allocation, a matching global lower bound over \(\mathcal A_\lambda\), certifies \((\lambda,\alpha)\in\mathcal B_{4,\alpha}\).  If two adjacent subcells carry verified certificates proving respectively \(\Delta_{4,\alpha}(\lambda)=0\) and \(\Delta_{4,\alpha}(\lambda)>0\), their common internal frontier is an actual boundary of \(\mathcal B_{4,\alpha}\); every point of that frontier is a real root of a basis-determinant, inactive-slack, residual-contact, or candidate-value-difference polynomial generated by the two certificates.
body.justification: This is the exact optimality certificate and finite boundary-candidate theorem needed to turn a phase diagram into mathematics.
body.gap: Mai supplies generic finite-convergence conditions, while the present equivalence must fuse a confidence LP saddle, privacy-face stationarity, and global residual positivity without assuming a rational optimizer.
body.consumer: It gives an independently checkable certificate format for choosing a private trial design and for auditing the privacy budget at which the optimal channel family changes.
body.proof_tex:
Work at a parameter point in a cell \(J\) satisfying the proposed statement.  Let \(u_\Gamma\) be the common primal and dual value certified for the displayed balanced binary candidate.  Primal feasibility gives
\[
 L^\star_{4,\alpha}(\lambda)\le u_\Gamma.
\]
For each allocation \(m\in\{1,2,3\}\), the certificate supplies a dual lower functional \(L_{\Gamma,m}(a)\) whose dual feasibility implies, by weak duality,
\[
 V_m(Q_a)\ge L_{\Gamma,m}(a)
 \qquad(a\in\mathcal A_\lambda).
\]
The globally certified residual is
\[
 r_{\Gamma,m}(a):=L_{\Gamma,m}(a)-u_\Gamma\ge0
 \qquad(a\in\mathcal A_\lambda).
\]
Therefore \(V_m(Q_a)\ge u_\Gamma\) for every allocation and staircase weight.  The staircase-refinement theorem says that every admissible finite-output channel is a postprocessing of some \(Q_a\), and hence has value no smaller than that \(Q_a\).  Taking all infima yields
\[
 L^\star_{4,\alpha}(\lambda)\ge u_\Gamma.
\]
Together with the candidate upper bound this is equality.  Because the candidate is a balanced binary randomized-response channel, the definition of \(\Delta\) now gives
\[
 0\le\Delta_{4,\alpha}(\lambda)
 \le u_\Gamma-L^\star_{4,\alpha}(\lambda)=0,
\]
so \((\lambda,\alpha)\in\mathcal B_{4,\alpha}\).  This is the claimed certificate sufficiency.

On \(J\), a fixed confidence-primal or confidence-dual basis is obtained by solving a fixed finite linear system.  Cramer's rule expresses every basic variable and objective as a rational function of \((\lambda,\alpha)\) and of any algebraic channel coordinates.  The assumed nonvanishing determinants make every division legal, and their fixed signs permit multiplication by denominators without reversing an inequality.  Complementary slackness, inactive slacks, active privacy faces, and candidate-value comparisons are therefore finitely many polynomial equalities and sign conditions.  The residual certificates are likewise finite polynomial identities and nonnegativity conditions.  Thus the region on which a particular certificate remains valid is semialgebraic by the cited projection result.

Suppose two adjacent certified subcells have respectively \(\Delta=0\) and \(\Delta>0\).  Continuity of \(\Delta\), proved in the polynomial-attainment theorem, shows that their common internal frontier is an actual relative boundary of \(\mathcal B_{4,\alpha}\).  Let \(p\) be a point on this frontier.  If every basis determinant, inactive slack, residual, and candidate-value difference generated by the two certificates were nonzero at \(p\), continuity of this finite family of polynomials would preserve all their signs in a neighborhood of \(p\).  The same active descriptions and the same conclusion about \(\Delta\) would then persist across \(p\), contradicting that the adjacent certified signs are different.  Hence at least one such polynomial vanishes at \(p\), which proves the boundary-root assertion in the narrowed statement.
